headlines.summary: The S&P 500 returned to an intraday record Tuesday as tech gains, easing oil prices and Treasury yields helped stocks overcome months of market shocks.
headlines.article_text: Chart: A look at the S&P 500's remarkable and defiant trip to a new record Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points S&P 500 surpassed its August peak on Tuesday. Stocks recovered despite the Iran war’s oil shock, rising borrowing costs and the Fed’s first rate hike. The market rally was also boosted by a few stocks tied to the AI hype, highlighting investors’ appetite for ambitious tech stocks. In this article .SPX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The S&P 500 rose to an all-time intraday on Tuesday, touching 7844.52 and surpassing its August 13 intraday peak when it hit 7,830. The benchmark also closed for the first time over 7,800. The recovery comes after months of oil shocks, rising borrowing costs and the possible start of a Federal Reserve rate hiking cycle. The record rally comes just a day after the 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5.3%, reaching levels not seen since 2002. In mid September, the Fed raised its benchmark rate for the first time in over three years and indicated more were to come. Oil had crossed $100 a barrel in early March for the first time since 2022 as the Iran conflict disrupted energy supplies moving through the Strait of Hormuz. After falling below $70 a barrel, it slingshot back above $100 in early September. "At the end of the day, oil and bond yields can be correlated, but so is the stock market and profits. And if the profits are there, which they have been, the stock market is going to be resilient, even if the economy is a bit more mixed," Shawn Snyder, economic strategist at Potomac Fund Management, told CNBC. Unlike prior records this year, this latest run has been narrowly lead by a few stocks tied to the AI hype and deemed unfettered by adverse macroeconomic headwinds. "When traders take a breather from the noise surrounding them — much of it negative in recent months — and look closer at what's happening in the markets, it becomes clear the U.S. stock market is the best place to park their money compared with other locations. It's hard to argue against the mostly positive risk-reward ratio we've seen over multiple decades," said JJ Kinahan, Cboe Global Markets senior vice president of retail and alternative investments. The so-called Magnificent 7 namely, Nvidia , Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , Meta , Microsoft and Tesla make up more than 34% of the market cap of the S&P 500 . "When you consider that much girth among a small handful of stocks, it's apparent how much these stocks' daily movements dictate the direction of the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, both of which are in record territory again today," Kinahan said. With tech companies investing heavily in data centers and computing infrastructure demand for chips and equipment has gone up. Earlier this year, Amazon said it expected about $200 billion in capital expenditures across its businesses in 2026, citing opportunities including AI, chips and robotics. Investor appetite for ambitious technology bets also became evident in June, when SpaceX raised $75 billion in the largest IPO ever and began trading on June 12. The debut became another milestone where investors continued backing growth companies despite higher energy prices and borrowing costs. Looking ahead, however, Potomac Fund Management's Snyder cautioned that the "weakening" market breadth may last longer if inflation shows no signs of easing, or if there's no clear signal that the Federal Reserve is achieving its mandate. The central bank is slated to release its minutes from the September meeting on Wednesday. The market "can look relatively calm, but there are still things going on underneath the surface that may not be so calm," Snyder said. headlines.article_text: Trump says MAGA Inc. PAC to pay for TV ads that praised him Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points President Donald Trump said he and his political action committee will pay for controversial television ads that praised him and had been funded by the U.S. government. The White House later clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service ads moving forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. Trump's announcement came after continued backlash to the ads, which had run in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election. A new Trump ad began airing on Tuesday. US President Donald Trump speaks in the East Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, Sept. 30, 2026. Jonathan Ernst | Reuters President Donald Trump hedged Tuesday when asked whether he would reimburse the U.S. government for previously aired television advertisements that praised him, saying, "We'll decide." The ads cost the federal government nearly $10 million before Trump on Monday announced that he and his political action committee will pay for the segments in the face of criticism that they are propaganda and aimed at helping Republican political candidates. The White House later Monday clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service announcements going forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. The prior airings reportedly were funded from a pool of up to $20 million set aside by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security . Asked whether he would reimburse the government for the costs of ads already aired, Trump told reporters, "The ads were really good." "They were promotion for the country, done by many presidents before," he said. "So we'll decide." Trump's latest comments on the furor came hours after a new ad aired. That ad was labeled as paid for by the U.S. government. The ad features video clips of Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussing the U.S. capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year. "Nicolás Maduro had his chance ... until he didn't," Hegseth says in the ad. "He effed around and he found out." Another clip in the ad shows Rubio warning, "Don't play games with [President Trump] in office." The ads have been running in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election . Those contests will determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans will maintain their majorities in both chambers of Congress. The White House and MAGA Inc. did not immediately reply when asked whether the super PAC would cover the cost of the new ad or whether the buy had already been placed before Trump's announcement and would remain taxpayer-funded. "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.," Trump said. AdImpact has tracked roughly $9.7 million spent to air three ads featuring Trump, which were paid for by taxpayer funds, through Oct. 5. Trump's announcement that he would pay for the ads came three days after The New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that "Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency." Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' The Times said federal money to pay for the ads became available on Sept. 19, "when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events." Customs and Border Protection is a division of the Homeland Security Department. Sen. Maggie Hassan , D-N.H., in a Sept. 24 letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, wrote, "The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates.'" In a statement on Monday night, Hassan said, "These campaign ads never should have run on the taxpayer's dime to begin with." "They were clearly wrong and clearly illegal, which is why the President should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent on these ads," Hassan said. "There's a lesson here: We can't underestimate the difference that citizens can make in our country when they speak out and hold their leaders to account," she said. On Tuesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., called for the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate the ads. "The government is not the President's campaign committee, and the Treasury is not his campaign account. The federal government has no legitimate business billing the public for campaign messaging that a candidate's political committee should pay for," Schumer wrote in a letter . Last week, the advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint urging the Federal Communications Commission, the Federal Trade Commission and TV broadcasters to stop airing the ads. Public Citizen previously asked the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate whether the ads violated federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act. That law restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns. MAGA Inc. has raised $424.4 million and spent $32.4 million during the 2025-26 cycle through Aug. 31, leaving the Trump Super PAC with $415.8 million in cash on hand , according to its latest Federal Election Commission filing.
